title: Lecture 3: Supply, Demand and Market Equilibrium
mainIdeas: Prices come from the interaction of buyers' demand and sellers' supply.
Markets move toward the price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
Shifts in demand or supply change the equilibrium price and quantity.

concepts.name: Law of demand
concepts.explanation: Holding everything else constant, when the price of a good rises, the quantity buyers want falls. The demand curve slopes downward because higher prices push buyers toward substitutes and stretch their budgets.
concepts.misconception: Thinking a higher price lowers demand, when it lowers quantity demanded. The curve itself does not move.
concepts.bridge: Raise ticket prices for a derby and fewer fans buy seats. Same fans, same love for the club, just fewer tickets at that price.

concepts.name: Law of supply
concepts.explanation: Holding everything else constant, when the price of a good rises, sellers offer more of it. Higher prices make extra production profitable, so the supply curve slopes upward.
concepts.misconception: Assuming supply means the amount actually sold, rather than what sellers are willing to offer at each price.
concepts.bridge: If shirt sales pay more, your startup would print more shirts. Higher margin, more effort put into supplying.

concepts.name: Market equilibrium
concepts.explanation: Equilibrium is the price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. At that price there is no pressure for the price to change, and the market clears.
concepts.misconception: Believing equilibrium is a fair or ideal price, rather than just the price where the two quantities match.
concepts.bridge: Like a transfer fee that both clubs finally accept: not fair, just the point where buyer and seller stop moving.

concepts.name: Shortage and surplus
concepts.explanation: Below equilibrium, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied: a shortage, which pushes prices up. Above equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded: a surplus, which pushes prices down.
concepts.misconception: Thinking a shortage means the good is rare, when it means the price is set too low.
concepts.bridge: Final tickets sold too cheap sell out in minutes and touts appear. That's a shortage created by the price, not by the stadium.

concepts.name: Shift vs movement along a curve
concepts.explanation: A change in the good's own price causes a movement along the curve. A change in anything else, like income, tastes or input costs, shifts the whole curve.
concepts.misconception: Saying a price change shifts the demand curve. Price only moves you along it.
concepts.bridge: A star signing makes fans want more shirts at every price: the curve shifts. A discount just moves fans along the same curve.

concepts.name: Effects of a demand shift on equilibrium
concepts.explanation: When demand increases with supply unchanged, both equilibrium price and quantity rise. When demand falls, both fall. The new equilibrium is where the new demand curve crosses supply.
concepts.misconception: Expecting price to rise but quantity to stay the same, forgetting sellers respond to the higher price.
concepts.bridge: Your club reaches the final, demand for your merch jumps, you charge more and print more. Price and quantity rise together.
